**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Religious Studies 3 (0785), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2019. Paper 3: The New Testament, Religion in Relation to Philosophy, Ethics and Morality, Historical Development of Islam (570CE-661CE). Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

The paper has six sections of six questions each: Section 2.1 The Gospel According to Luke (questions 1-6); Section 2.2 The Fourth Gospel (questions 7-12); Section 2.3 The Early Church as Reflected in Acts and 1 Corinthians (questions 13-18); Section 4.1 Philosophy of Religion (questions 19-24); Section 4.2 Ethics and Morality (questions 25-30); Section 6.0 The Historical Development of Islam (570CE - 661CE) (questions 31-36).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Sujet scanné de trois pages (page de garde puis 36 questions en six sections de six) : filigrane gcerevision.com et texte fantôme du verso ignorés ; aucune question illisible, aucune figure ni carte. Les doubles espaces imprimés ont été normalisés.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level, avec des références bibliques ou islamiques limitées à celles que l'auteur tient pour sûres ; formulations prudentes (« according to Islamic tradition », « Christians believe »). À faire relire par un spécialiste (théologie chrétienne, histoire de l'islam, philosophie de la religion) avant mise en avant.

Question 35 : le point de vue chiite sur la désignation d'Ali est exposé de façon neutre ; le récit du Saqifa et des guerres de la Ridda suit la tradition sunnite classique ; la question de Fadak n'est pas traitée.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Examine the problems that arose following the death of Prophet Muhammad.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Prophet Muhammad died in AD 632 (11 AH) in Medina, having united most of Arabia under Islam. He left no male heir and, according to the Sunni view, no explicit instruction on who should lead the community after him. His death created several serious problems for the young community.

**1. Shock and disbelief.** Many Muslims could not accept that the Prophet had died. Umar is reported to have denied it at first. Abu Bakr calmed the people by reminding them that Muhammad was a messenger like the messengers before him, and that whoever worshipped Muhammad should know that Muhammad was dead, but God is alive and does not die. This restored order.

**2. The problem of succession.**
- Who was to lead the community? While the family of the Prophet was preparing for his burial, some of the Ansar met in the hall (*saqifa*) of the Banu Sa'ida to choose a leader from among themselves.
- Abu Bakr, Umar and Abu Ubayda went there. The Muhajirun argued that the leadership belonged to the Quraysh, whom the Arabs would accept, and Umar and others offered their allegiance to Abu Bakr. Others, including some Ansar, accepted. Abu Bakr was thus chosen as the first caliph (*khalifa*, successor).
- Some Muslims, later known as the Shi'a, hold that the Prophet had designated Ali, his cousin and son-in-law, as his successor, and that Ali was not consulted. Ali and members of the Prophet's family are reported to have delayed their pledge of allegiance. This difference of view over the right to leadership became the root of the later division into Sunni and Shi'a, which still exists.
- The question of the nature of the office was also new: the caliph was to rule but had no claim to prophethood or revelation.

**3. The wars of apostasy (*Ridda*).**
- Some tribes refused to pay *zakat* (the alms tax), claiming that their agreement with the Prophet was personal and had ended with his death. Others left Islam altogether.
- False prophets arose, such as Musaylima in Yamama, Tulayha among the Banu Asad, al-Aswad al-Ansi in Yemen, and the woman Sajah. They threatened the unity and the religion of the community.
- Abu Bakr decided to fight, saying that he would fight those who separated prayer from *zakat*. He organised armies under commanders such as Khalid ibn al-Walid, and in about a year had restored the authority of Medina over Arabia. The battle of Yamama was costly, since many reciters of the Qur'an were killed.

**4. Security on the borders.** The expedition of Usama against the Byzantine frontier, which the Prophet had prepared, was left in doubt: some wished to cancel it. Abu Bakr carried it out, and it deterred the border tribes.

**5. The preservation of the Qur'an.** The loss of many reciters at Yamama led Umar to fear for the Qur'an, and the compilation under Abu Bakr was one result.

**6. Administrative and leadership problems.** The new caliph had to run the community without the Prophet's authority, to settle disputes, to manage the treasury and to keep the loyalty of the tribes who had accepted Islam recently. Some tribes had regarded their agreement as a pact with a person.

**Conclusion.** The death of the Prophet led to a crisis of faith, a dispute over succession, the rebellion of the tribes and the rise of false prophets. Abu Bakr's firm leadership solved most of the problems in two years, but the question of the legitimate leadership remained a source of division in later history.
